Upper Respiratory Tract Pathology

Dr. Walter L. Kemp, MD, PhD — SDL Lecture
PATH · Deep Dive with Histology

Session Objectives

  1. Describe acute rhinitis, allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinitis, nasal polyps, acute sinusitis/rhinosinusitis, and chronic obstructive rhinosinusitis with regards to etiology, clinical presentation, and pathology
  2. Describe necrotizing lesions of the upper airways including fungal infections, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and cocaine inhalation
  3. Compare and contrast pharyngitis, tonsillitis, epiglottitis, and laryngitis
  4. Describe the demographics, morphology, and important features of angiofibroma, olfactory neuroblastoma, sinonasal papilloma, NUT midline carcinoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma
  5. Describe the clinical and pathologic features of non-neoplastic and neoplastic conditions of the larynx
  6. Describe otitis media and its complications

1. Rhinitis (Acute, Allergic, Chronic)

Rhinitis = inflammation (-itis) of the nose (rhin-). Symptoms: nasal congestion with discharge, sneezing, can progress to sore throat/postnasal drip. Upper respiratory structures are anatomically continuous and interconnected — inflammation rarely stays confined to one site, which is why rhinitis can lead into sinusitis or otitis media.

Acute Infectious (Viral)Acute Infectious (Bacterial)AllergicChronic
EtiologyAdenovirus, Echovirus, Rhinovirus (the "common cold" agents)β-hemolytic streptococciPlants, fungi, animalsRepeated acute rhinitis (infectious or allergic)
MorphologyThickened, edematous mucosa; narrowed nasal cavities; watery/runny dischargeSame as viral, but with purulent discharge (neutrophils now driving the exudate)Same as viral but with prominent eosinophilsNasal polyps/deviated septum; neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells (chronic inflammatory infiltrate with tissue remodeling)
Pattern to remember — Viral = watery/fluid discharge. Bacterial = purulent (neutrophil-driven). Allergic = eosinophil-driven. Chronic = mixed chronic inflammatory cells (macrophages, lymphocytes) with fibrosis/structural change (deviated septum, polyps) from repeated acute episodes.

USMLE-Style Question

A 7-year-old boy presents with several days of nasal congestion, clear watery rhinorrhea, and sneezing. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

A. Group A β-hemolytic streptococcus
B. Rhinovirus
C. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
D. Aspergillus fumigatus
E. Mucor species
Answer: B. Rhinovirus (along with adenovirus and echovirus) is the classic cause of viral acute rhinitis — the "common cold" — producing watery discharge from mucosal edema and vasodilation rather than a neutrophilic purulent exudate.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with several years of recurrent nasal congestion is found to have a nasal polyp on exam. Which histologic finding would be most expected on biopsy of the polyp?

A. Granulomas with giant cells
B. Edematous stroma with hyperplastic mucinous glands and inflammatory cells
C. Sheets of small round blue cells with neuroendocrine markers
D. Non-septate, right-angle branching hyphae invading vessels
E. Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges
Answer: B. A nasal polyp shows nonspecific edematous (edematous) stroma with hyperplastic mucinous glands and an inflammatory infiltrate — a reactive process rather than a specific diagnostic entity. Without clinical context, a pathologist often cannot distinguish it from other inflammatory nasal tissue on morphology alone.

2. Nasal Polyps

Appearance: edematous stroma with hyperplastic mucinous glands and an inflammatory infiltrate (neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, sometimes eosinophils if allergic in origin). It is a nonspecific inflammatory morphology — many different reactive processes look identical under the microscope, so a pathologist blinded to clinical history often could not name the lesion from tissue alone.

Complications: can physically obstruct the nasal airway, and because the paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity, an obstructing polyp impairs sinus drainage — directly predisposing to sinusitis.

Why this matters clinically — This is a concrete example of how upper airway structures are functionally linked: a polyp is not just a local nuisance, it is a mechanical setup for a second disease process (sinusitis) downstream.

3. Sinusitis

Description: inflammation of the paranasal sinuses. Types: acute and chronic (chronic = persistent/recurrent symptoms that don't resolve; sinuses are a somewhat protected/enclosed space, so chronic sinusitis can be notoriously difficult to clear).

Complications

  • Empyema of the sinus — entrapment of purulent exudate within the sinus cavity
  • Mucocele — accumulation of mucus, forming a mucus-filled cystic space (mucus-producing glands keep secreting into an obstructed space)
  • Osteomyelitis — the bony sinus wall is thin; sustained inflammation can erode through it, spreading infection into bone
  • Spread through bone into the cranial cavity → meningitis; inflammation around vessels can also cause thrombosis
Board pearl — Most acute/chronic rhinitis and sinusitis is diagnosed clinically; pathologists rarely examine microscopic sections of it unless surgical tissue is excised as part of treatment (in which case it is still sent to pathology, regardless of how unremarkable it's expected to be).

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with poorly controlled chronic sinusitis develops sudden headache, fever, and altered mental status. Imaging shows erosion through the posterior wall of a paranasal sinus with intracranial extension. Which complication has occurred?

A. Empyema of the sinus
B. Mucocele
C. Meningitis from transosseous spread
D. Allergic fungal sinusitis
E. Nasal polyposis
Answer: C. Chronic sinus inflammation can erode through the thin bony sinus wall and spread directly into the cranial cavity, producing meningitis — one of the most feared complications of sinusitis given its proximity to the brain.

4. Necrotizing Lesions of the Upper Airway

Four processes classically cause necrotizing/destructive lesions of the nose and upper airway: acute fungal infections, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, and cocaine inhalation. GPA is covered in depth under vasculitis; the focus here is fungal infection and cocaine-related necrosis.

Acute Fungal Infections

Zygomycetes (Rhizopus, Mucor)Non-septate hyphae, branch at wide (~90°) angles
AspergillusSeptate hyphae, classically branch at 45° angles
Fastest way to tell them apart — Branching angle (45° vs. wide/right angle) can be genuinely hard to judge under the scope. The presence or absence of septae is the clearest, most reliable distinguishing feature: septate = Aspergillus; non-septate = Zygomycetes.

Patients affected: immunocompromised hosts — neutropenic patients, stem cell transplant recipients, those on long-term corticosteroids, and patients with HIV/AIDS or other immunocompromising disease.

Important point: Zygomycetes are notorious for invading blood vessels — this can cause thrombosis (→ downstream infarction) or hemorrhage (from vessel wall damage). They can also invade locally into adjacent structures, including bone.

Classic association — Patients in diabetic ketoacidosis are specifically known for developing fulminant rhinocerebral mucormycosis — a board-favorite pairing.
Zygomycete infection of the lung — thrombosed vessels
Gross cut surface of lung near the hilum. The yellow-tan, rounded, firm structures plugging several vessel lumens are thrombi — the direct consequence of fungal invasion of the vessel wall. The lecturer emphasized this finding specifically to illustrate the vascular-invasion behavior of Zygomycetes: once the fungus invades the vessel, thrombosis follows, and downstream tissue is put at risk for infarction (or hemorrhage if the vessel wall itself is disrupted).

Cocaine-Induced Necrosis

Cocaine is a potent vasoconstrictor. Chronic vasoconstriction of nasal mucosal tissue impairs oxygen delivery, causing tissue death — classically producing a perforated nasal septum. This is a recognized finding in forensic pathology, though it is only one of several possible causes (GPA and fungal infection can also perforate the septum, so the finding alone is not cocaine-specific).

A Related Aside: IV Drug Use and Pulmonary Foreign Material

When people inject drugs intravenously, insoluble filler/foreign material injected along with the drug embolizes to the lungs and deposits in small vessels, provoking a foreign-body reaction and progressive fibrosis. This can become quite extensive over time.

H&E — foreign material in lung
Hemorrhagic, congested lung parenchyma with pale gray-green, somewhat crystalline-appearing foreign material embedded within the tissue (left-center) surrounded by an inflammatory reaction.
Same section, polarized light
The identical field viewed under polarized light: the foreign material lights up brightly (birefringence), confirming it is particulate/crystalline filler rather than tissue. The lecturer specifically walked through this paired H&E-vs-polarized comparison to demonstrate how polarized microscopy is used to confirm foreign material that might otherwise be easy to overlook on routine H&E.

USMLE-Style Question

A neutropenic patient recovering from induction chemotherapy develops facial pain and a black eschar on the hard palate. Biopsy shows broad, ribbon-like hyphae without septae invading blood vessels. Which organism is most likely?

A. Aspergillus fumigatus
B. Rhizopus species
C. Candida albicans
D. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
E. Histoplasma capsulatum
Answer: B. Non-septate ("ribbon-like") hyphae with a tendency for angioinvasion in a neutropenic host is classic for a Zygomycete such as Rhizopus (mucormycosis). Aspergillus would show septate hyphae instead.

5. Pharyngitis, Tonsillitis, Epiglottitis, Laryngitis

These four are best thought of together — infections of the nasopharynx/oropharynx region — because they are anatomically contiguous, and it's common for one process (especially viral) to spread and involve more than one site simultaneously.

EntityKey Features
PharyngitisSore throat; frequently accompanies a more widespread upper respiratory tract infection
TonsillitisIf caused by β-hemolytic streptococci → risk of peritonsillar abscess, glomerulonephritis, and acute rheumatic fever as post-streptococcal complications
EpiglottitisOften associated with H. influenzae; abrupt onset; can cause airway obstruction with loss of the airway (the epiglottis normally protects the trachea during swallowing — when it becomes acutely inflamed and swollen, it can occlude the airway itself)
LaryngitisSee breakdown below — bacterial, viral, chemical, or specific-organism causes
Remember the streptococcal connections — β-hemolytic strep ties together tonsillitis (peritonsillar abscess), the heart (acute rheumatic fever), and the kidney (glomerulonephritis) — a useful thread across multiple organ systems.
Acute epiglottitis — gross
Markedly swollen, diffusely erythematous ("cherry red") epiglottis from a fatal case of acute bacterial epiglottitis.
Acute epiglottitis — histology
The dark purple band on the left is the surface mucosa, with visibly dilated, congested blood vessels beneath it. The sea of small dark dots filling the right two-thirds of the field is a dense neutrophilic infiltrate — confirming acute bacterial inflammation. This case was fatal: the swelling from this exact process caused fatal airway obstruction.

Laryngitis — Specific Causes

  • Can be caused by bacterial, viral, or chemical sources; often part of a more widespread upper respiratory infection
  • Tuberculous laryngitis — from coughed-up sputum containing caseating, necrotic mycobacteria; the sputum is effectively re-aspirated onto the larynx, seeding infection there
  • Diphtheric laryngitis (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) — an exotoxin causes tissue necrosis, which combines with a fibrinopurulent exudate to form a pseudomembrane. This pseudomembrane can dislodge and travel down the airway, causing obstruction.
  • Parainfluenza and RSV — cause croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), producing stridor and a harsh cough. Usually self-limited, but the degree of stridor from breathing against a narrowed airway can be alarming, and it is occasionally fatal.
Laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) — cross-section, fatal pediatric case
Cross-section through the airway of a child who died from laryngotracheobronchitis. The cartilage rings of the airway wall are visible, but the airway lumen is almost completely obliterated by markedly thickened mucosa (the pale, folded tissue filling the center) — the thickened mucosa would be expected to show inflammatory cells, congestion, and edema on microscopy. A separate, smaller slit-like structure adjacent to the airway represents the esophagus. This image was used to show just how severely the mucosal thickening of croup can compromise the airway — enough, in this case, to cause the child's death.

USMLE-Style Question

A 4-year-old presents with a harsh, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness following several days of a viral upper respiratory illness. Which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible?

A. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis
C. Parainfluenza virus
D. Haemophilus influenzae
E. Rhizopus species
Answer: C. This is the classic presentation of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus (RSV is another common cause). Diphtheria would show a gray pseudomembrane; H. influenzae causes epiglottitis with a more abrupt, toxic presentation.

USMLE-Style Question

An unimmunized child develops a sore throat, low-grade fever, and a thick gray membrane over the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when scraped. Which of the following best explains the membrane's formation?

A. Non-septate fungal hyphae invading the mucosa
B. Exotoxin-mediated necrosis combined with a fibrinopurulent exudate
C. Eosinophilic infiltration of the mucosa
D. Thrombosis of submucosal vessels from cocaine use
E. Viral cytopathic effect with syncytial giant cell formation
Answer: B. This is diphtheria: the C. diphtheriae exotoxin causes local tissue necrosis, which combines with a fibrinopurulent exudate to form the characteristic adherent gray pseudomembrane — a membrane that can dislodge and obstruct the airway if displaced.

6. Sinonasal & Nasopharyngeal Neoplasms

Five entities to know by their characteristic demographics — on a test, the demographic clue is often what identifies the answer, since these lesions can otherwise overlap in presentation.

EntityDemographicsMorphologyImportant Points
Nasopharyngeal angiofibromaAdolescent males; fair-skinned, red-haired (and associated with FAP)Highly vascular, fibrous neoplasmCannot metastasize, but can be locally aggressive — can extend intracranially (e.g., through the cribriform plate). Bleeds profusely; patients can exsanguinate from it.
Sinonasal papillomaMales; 30–60 yearsExophytic (grows outward), endophytic (grows inward/inverted), or cylindrical in shapeLocally aggressive — can invade the orbit or cranial vault. Exophytic and endophytic forms are associated with HPV.
Olfactory neuroblastomaBimodal: ~15 and ~50 yearsSmall round blue cell tumorNeuroendocrine — expresses neuron-specific enolase, synaptophysin, CD56 (and/or chromogranin). Think "neuroblastoma → neuroendocrine markers."
NUT midline carcinomaAny ageLooks like squamous cell carcinomaVery aggressive. Driven by a fusion of NUT (a chromatin regulator) to BRD4 (a chromatin reader) — the fusion amplifies proliferation; if the fusion is disrupted, tumor cells terminally differentiate (a mechanistic detail that's occasionally tested).
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaAfrica: children · China: adults (rare in children) · US: rare in bothKeratinizing squamous cell, non-keratinizing squamous cell, or undifferentiated/basaloidAssociated with EBV (most closely with the undifferentiated form), nitrosamines, and smoking. Despite being aggressive-appearing, it carries a relatively good prognosis.
Basaloid pattern reminder — Think of the basal layer of stratified squamous epithelium: high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, small hyperchromatic nuclei, minimal keratin — very different from superficial squamous cells (large, pink, keratin-filled, small nucleus). The undifferentiated/basaloid form of nasopharyngeal carcinoma resembles this basal pattern and has the strongest EBV association.

USMLE-Style Question

A 16-year-old fair-skinned adolescent male presents with recurrent, severe epistaxis and nasal obstruction. Imaging shows a highly vascular mass in the nasopharynx with extension toward the skull base. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
B. Olfactory neuroblastoma
C. Sinonasal papilloma
D. NUT midline carcinoma
E. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Answer: A. The classic demographic (adolescent, fair-skinned male) plus profuse bleeding from a highly vascular nasopharyngeal mass with local extension is the textbook presentation of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

USMLE-Style Question

A sinonasal small round blue cell tumor stains positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and CD56. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Sinonasal papilloma
B. Olfactory neuroblastoma
C. Squamous cell carcinoma
D. NUT midline carcinoma
E. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Answer: B. Olfactory neuroblastoma is a neuroendocrine small round blue cell tumor, characteristically expressing neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin, chromogranin, and CD56.

7. Non-Neoplastic & Neoplastic Conditions of the Larynx

Non-Neoplastic Lesions

EntityEtiologyMorphologyImportant Point
Vocal cord (singer's) nodulesSmokers/singersBilateral; smooth, rounded growth on the vocal cord; squamous epithelium over fibrous stromaSome sources lump nodules and polyps together as one entity
Vocal cord polypsSmokers/singersUnilateral; smooth, rounded growth on the vocal cord; squamous epithelium over fibrous stromaSame lesion as above, just unilateral instead of bilateral
Squamous papilloma/papillomatosisHPV 6 and 11 (low-risk types)Finger-like projections covered by squamous epithelium over a fibrovascular coreCan be recurrent and multiple, most commonly in children; low risk of malignant transformation, but recurrence can necessitate repeated airway surgery
Shape is the key differentiator on gross/microscopic exam — nodules/polyps have a smooth surface; squamous papilloma has finger-like (papillary) projections, like the fingers of a cross-sectioned glove.
Incidental laryngeal nodule — false cord
An incidental autopsy finding: a small, smooth-surfaced nodule seen arising from the false vocal cord (not the true cord). The lecturer used this as a live "what is this" exercise — the smooth surface (rather than finger-like projections) points away from squamous papilloma toward a vocal cord nodule/polyp-type lesion, illustrating that not everything found incidentally fits neatly into the textbook categories.

Carcinoma of the Larynx

  • Description: most often squamous cell carcinoma (rarely adenocarcinoma, since minor glands are present in the larynx)
  • Demographics: males, >50 years
  • Etiology: smoking (or smoking + alcohol, which is synergistic); also radiation, asbestosis, HPV infection
  • Pathogenesis: hyperplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma — a repeated stimulus (viral, or chemical/smoking-related damage) drives cells to divide repeatedly; accumulating replication errors produce dysplasia, and further accumulated errors produce cells capable of invasion and metastasis (carcinoma)
  • Location: ~3/4 arise on the vocal cords; otherwise supraglottic (abundant lymphatics) is more common than infraglottic (minimal lymphatics)
  • Pathology: classic squamous cell carcinoma features — intercellular bridges and keratin pearls
  • Clinical: hoarseness is the most common presentation, because most tumors sit on the vocal cords and change the voice early; potential airway obstruction with large/advanced tumors
Location determines how early it's caught — vocal cord tumors present early (hoarseness) because they immediately affect voice. Supraglottic tumors have abundant lymphatics, so they are more likely to have already spread to lymph nodes by the time they're identified — often once airway obstruction has developed. Infraglottic tumors have minimal lymphatics and are less likely to spread early, but for the same reason as supraglottic, are also more likely to first present with more advanced local disease (obstruction) or hemoptysis if they become necrotic.
Leukoplakia of the vocal cord — gross
Opened larynx showing a discrete white patch on the vocal cord. Leukoplakia is a purely descriptive clinical term ("white patch") and is nonspecific — it can represent anything from a fungal infection to a reactive process, to dysplasia, to frank carcinoma. It always requires biopsy to determine what it actually is.
Squamous dysplasia — histology
On the left, squamous cells show normal maturation: regular size and shape, smaller and paler nuclei as cells approach the surface. On the right, the epithelium is dysplastic — nuclei are more hyperchromatic, irregular in size and shape, and maturation toward the surface is disordered. Critically, the basement membrane remains intact and there is no invasion through it — this is still dysplasia, not carcinoma. The lecturer specifically framed this as a side-by-side comparison to teach the visual distinction between normal maturation and dysplastic change.
Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma — gross
Ulcerated, irregular white-tan tumor with linear surface striations, seen eroding beyond its site of origin in the larynx into adjacent tissue (the epiglottis is visible unopened in this view). This demonstrates the locally destructive, ulcerating growth pattern typical of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma once it has progressed beyond dysplasia.

USMLE-Style Question

Which of the following features distinguishes carcinoma in situ (severe dysplasia) from invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx on histology?

A. Presence of keratin pearls
B. Nuclear hyperchromasia
C. Intact basement membrane with no invasion beyond it
D. Presence of intercellular bridges
E. Disordered cellular maturation
Answer: C. The defining feature separating dysplasia (even severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ) from invasive carcinoma is whether the basement membrane remains intact. Once tumor cells breach the basement membrane, the lesion is, by definition, invasive carcinoma.

USMLE-Style Question

A 68-year-old male smoker with a 40-year history of alcohol use presents with 3 months of progressive hoarseness. Laryngoscopy reveals a mass on the true vocal cord. Which histologic feature would confirm a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma?

A. Non-septate hyphae invading vessels
B. Small round blue cells with neuroendocrine markers
C. Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges
D. Fibrovascular cores lined by squamous epithelium
E. Highly vascular fibrous stroma
Answer: C. Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are the classic histologic hallmarks of squamous cell carcinoma — the most common malignancy of the larynx, strongly associated with smoking and alcohol use, and classically presenting with hoarseness when it arises on the vocal cords, as in this vignette.

8. Otitis Media & Complications

Description: inflammation of the middle ear; can be acute or chronic. Extremely common in childhood.

Complications

  • Meningitis — infection can erode directly through the thin bone separating the middle ear from the cranial cavity, seeding the meninges. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a classic causative organism for both the otitis media and the resulting meningitis.
  • Cholesteatoma — a complication of chronic otitis media: a benign, keratin-filled cystic structure lined by squamous epithelium that forms within the middle ear, grossly showing coalesced cholesterol clefts. Although histologically benign, its location within the middle ear means it can still cause real damage locally, including hearing loss, through pressure erosion of surrounding structures.
Same theme as sinusitis — once again, a middle-ear infection erodes through adjacent thin bone to reach the cranial cavity. This transosseous spread pattern (sinusitis → meninges, otitis media → meninges) is a recurring board theme for upper respiratory/ENT infections.

USMLE-Style Question

A 5-year-old with a history of recurrent otitis media develops progressive conductive hearing loss. Otoscopic exam reveals a pearly, keratin-debris-filled mass in the middle ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Acute mastoiditis
B. Cholesteatoma
C. Meningioma
D. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
E. Squamous papilloma
Answer: B. Cholesteatoma is a benign, keratin-filled squamous-lined mass that develops as a complication of chronic otitis media, and can cause conductive hearing loss and local bone erosion despite being histologically benign.

10. Closing Vignette

USMLE-Style Question (Lecture Closing Case)

A 62-year-old male with a 40-pack-year smoking history who consumes 1 L of alcohol per day presents to the emergency room because he is coughing up blood. His friend reports that he has gotten hoarser and harder to understand over the past month. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Chronic sinusitis
B. Singer's nodules
C. Chronic intravenous drug use
D. Laryngeal carcinoma
E. Stroke
Answer: D. Older male, heavy smoking and alcohol use, progressive hoarseness, and hemoptysis together point to laryngeal carcinoma — smoking and alcohol are the classic risk factors, and hoarseness reflects a vocal cord origin (the most common site), with hemoptysis suggesting mucosal ulceration/necrosis of the tumor.
